title: Our Advocate, the Old Command, and the Antichrists
summary: John writes so that his readers will not sin, but if they do, they have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for their sins and for the whole world. Knowing God shows in keeping his commands and loving one's brother. John encourages every age group in the church, warns against loving the world, and then addresses the painful departure of those he calls antichrists, who deny that Jesus is the Christ. The faithful have the anointing of the Spirit and should remain in what they heard from the beginning.
story: Chapter 1 ended with the honest admission that believers sin and the promise that God forgives those who confess. Chapter 2 opens by guarding against a wrong conclusion: the aim is not to sin. It then introduces the first of the letter's great tests, obedience and love, and in verses 18-27 names the crisis behind the letter for the first time. A group has left the fellowship, and John explains what their departure means and how the people who stayed can be confident that they know the truth. The chapter ends by looking ahead to Christ's appearing, preparing for chapter 3's reflection on being God's children.
historical:
Verse 19 is the clearest historical clue in the letter: they went out from us. There had been a schism, and those who left apparently claimed superior spiritual knowledge. John says their leaving showed they had never truly belonged. Their teaching, as verse 22 describes it, denied that Jesus is the Christ. In the context of the letter this was probably not a Jewish denial that Jesus was the Messiah, but a denial that the man Jesus was himself the divine Christ, such as the view Irenaeus attributes to Cerinthus, that a heavenly Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross.

The word antichrist appears in the Bible only in the letters of John (1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3; 2 John 7). John's readers had heard that the antichrist was coming, likely drawing on teaching such as Jesus' warnings about false messiahs (Mark 13:22) and Paul's description of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). John's surprising move is to say that many antichrists have already appeared, and that their presence shows it is the last hour.
cultural:
An advocate (parakletos) in the Greek world was someone called alongside to help, often a friend or patron who spoke for a person in a legal setting. John's Gospel uses the same word for the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus calls another Advocate (John 14:16). Here the advocate is Jesus himself, pleading with the Father for sinners, not as a lawyer arguing innocence but as the one whose sacrifice covers the guilt.

The address to children, fathers, and young men (verses 12-14) reflects a household way of speaking common in the ancient world, where an elder teacher could call disciples his children. Scholars debate whether John means three age groups in the church, two groups (fathers and young men) with children as a name for all believers, or three stages of spiritual maturity. The anointing (chrisma) of verses 20 and 27 draws on the Old Testament practice of anointing kings, priests, and prophets with oil. Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit, given to all believers, though some see it as the word of the gospel they received.
literary: The chapter mixes John's familiar method of claims and tests with a more lyrical passage. Three times John examines a claim (verses 4, 6, 9): the one who says he knows God, abides in him, or is in the light must show it in obedience and love. Verses 12-14 form a poem-like unit of six parallel lines addressed to children, fathers, and young men, first with I am writing, then with I have written. The warning about the world (verses 15-17) names three desires, the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life, which many readers have compared with the temptation in Eden (Genesis 3:6). Verses 18-27 are framed by the contrast between those who went out and those who remain, and the verb remain (meno) carries the section.

outline.t: Christ our advocate and atoning sacrifice
Knowing God shows in obedience and love
Words to children, fathers, and young men
Remain in Christ until he appears

doctrines.note: Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only ours but those of the whole world (verse 2). His death deals with sin before God, and he now speaks for his people before the Father.
To deny that Jesus is the Christ is to deny both the Father and the Son (verses 22-23). For John, what one believes about Jesus is not a side issue; it determines whether one has God at all.
Believers have an anointing from the Holy One, which teaches them and gives them knowledge of the truth. This is widely read as the Spirit, who keeps the church in the apostolic message.
Loving the world, meaning the whole system of life organized without God, competes with love for the Father. The world and its desires are passing away; only those who do God's will remain.

words.note: Hilasmos, atoning sacrifice or propitiation. The word group in Greek normally referred to turning away anger or making amends. In the twentieth century C. H. Dodd argued that in the Bible it means expiation, the removal of sin, while Leon Morris argued that it includes propitiation, the satisfying of God's just wrath. Many now see both ideas: God himself provides the sacrifice that removes sin and so turns away his judgment.

Meno, to remain, abide, or stay, used eleven times in this chapter. It is one of John's key words: the faithful remain in the Son and the Father, the word remains in them, and those who left did not remain. It describes a settled, continuing relationship rather than a single moment.

Antichristos, antichrist. The prefix anti can mean against or in place of, so an antichrist opposes Christ or sets himself up as a substitute. John applies the word to teachers who deny the Father and the Son, and to a spirit already at work in the world.

christ: The chapter presents Jesus in three roles. He is the Righteous One who speaks to the Father on behalf of sinners, an advocate who does not plead innocence but presents his own sacrifice. He is the atoning sacrifice, whose death deals with sin not only for one community but for the whole world. And he is the pattern: whoever claims to abide in him must walk as he walked. The chapter ends with Christ's coming, when believers who remain in him will stand before him with confidence rather than shame. Denying that Jesus is the Christ is the mark of antichrist; confessing the Son is to have the Father too.

hard.q: If Christ is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, will everyone be saved?
hard.a: Verse 2 is one of the most discussed verses in debates about the scope of Christ's work. Christians agree that it does not teach universalism, since the same letter says that whoever does not have the Son does not have life (5:12). Beyond that, they differ. Many, including Arminian and much of Lutheran and evangelical thought, read it as teaching that Christ died for every person without exception, providing a sacrifice sufficient for all and offered to all, which is received by faith. Those who hold to particular or definite atonement, common in Reformed theology, read whole world as meaning people from every nation and not only John's community or Israel, in the same way John 11:52 speaks of gathering God's scattered children into one. Some mediating views say that Christ's death is sufficient for all but effective for those who believe. All agree that John's purpose is to widen the readers' horizon: the cross is not a private possession of one group, and its reach is as wide as the world.

questions: John says he writes so that his readers will not sin, and then that if anyone sins they have an advocate. How do those two statements belong together in your own life?
The world's desires are described as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life. Which of these most shapes the choices around you?
Those who left claimed deeper knowledge. What does it mean for you to remain in what you heard from the beginning without becoming closed to learning?
